newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE-Euro bankers wrestle with EMU policy tools.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Euro bankers wrestle with EMU policy tools.

text.p: Debate in Europe is heating up over the framework the embryonic European Central Bank (ECB) should adopt in setting monetary policy for a single currency as the clock ticks towards its January 1, 1999 launch.

Talks at the Frankfurt-based European Monetary Institute -- the forerunner of the ECB -- have been cloaked in secrecy, but senior bankers on the continent agree the new institution will bear an uncanny resemblance to the Bundesbank.

The ECB will almost certainly adopt a German-style sale and repurchase system (repo) as its main tool for adjusting liquidity and interest rates. Like the Bundesbank, it will also favour money supply targets over inflation as the route to its goal of price stability, although a combination is possible.
But bankers say one thorny issue still divides the countries most likely to take part in the first wave of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) -- minimum reserve requirements.
"This is the main bone of contention...the Bundesbank clearly favours such an instrument and wants it in the toolbox of the ECB," Werner Becker, senior economist at Deutsche Bank in Frankfurt said.

The Bundesbank is the only central bank in Europe to insist on significant non-interest bearing reserve requirements, which restrict credit in its domestic market. Other central banks have only token requirements that have little effect on the domestic banking industry.
German banks are lobbying hard for the requirements, which have been pared sharply in recent years, to be scaled down even further to give them a competitive edge ahead of EMU.
Non-German banks are baulking furiously at the mere idea of EMU reserve requirements in belief they will be most affected.
"German banks have become used to reserve requirements so they would profit," Carlo Demeyer, senior Treasury economist at ABN Amro in Amsterdam said.
"It will put us at a disadvantage, especially if they (any requirements) are non-interest bearing," he said.
German banks must hold between 1.5 and two percent of the short-term money they borrows from foreign banks and domestic non-banks in non-interest bearing deposits at the Bundesbank.

The Bank of England, which attracted large numbers of foreign banks by ditching its reserve requirements years ago, has fought hard against reinstating them under EMU. The BOE says they are effectively a tax on banks and distort the relationship between broad money growth and inflation.

European bankers maintain the Bundesbank will get its way on this issue but will compromise by paying some interest on the reserves. However, this throws up another question -- will the interest be below or at market rates?
"Market-oriented interest rates is a more probable outcome because otherwise, there will be a distortion of competition between EMU and non-EMU banks," Becker said.
Far less contentious is the issue of how the ECB, which will eventually replace the EMI, will operate in its money market.
"Everyone agrees there should be an interest rate band with a lombard or penal lending rate at the top and a deposit rate at the bottom," one European central banker said.
"Local market operations would be conducted between those two bands, and there could be both a long- and a short-term repo," the central banker said.

Normally, the Bundesbank uses a fortnightly repo on a weekly basis to adjust liquidity in its money markets, setting either a fixed or variable interest rate to signal direction. It intervenes with a repo of shorter duration if this is warranted.
The French, Dutch, Irish and British central banks all operate more frequently in their money markets, and some European banks are hoping the ECB will follow suit.

"I would prefer the ECB to be active in the money market every day in order to know where the liquidity is. But for the time being, we don't have a clear answer," Philippe Ithurbide, chief economist at Societe Generale in Paris said.
Discussion centres on the duration of repos within the EMU system, with some suggestion of a two- or six-month facility to complement a more normal short-term instrument, bankers said.

The EMI, which currently groups central bankers from across Europe, has set a deadline for agreeing to the entire monetary policy framework by the end of 1996. A spokeswoman for the EMI said a detailed announcement would be made at that time.
On a broader scale, there has been argument over whether the ECB should choose money supply or inflation as its intermediate target for the ultimate aim of monetary union, price stability.

This ties in with the complex problem of harmonising monetary and inflation indicators, but bankers say there is little dissent among those countries most likely to join EMU in 1999 -- Germany, France, the Netherlands, Austria and Belgium.
Dutch Central Bank President Wim Duisenberg, who is expected to be the first head of the ECB after taking over the EMI in July 1997, has made clear which approach he prefers.

"For a direct inflation objective, it is not clear beforehand on which information policy decisions are based. The direct inflation strategy therefore, does not score very high in respect of transparency and possibility to justify decisions," he said.

The Bank of England opposes using money supply as a target because the indicator has proved unreliable across Europe in recent months, growing above target levels despite subdued inflation. Changes in techniques of money transmission were partly responsible, and it would be unwise to focus on such an untested aggregate at the start of EMU, the Bank maintains.
Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing has said there was no need for a rigid decision.

"A decision cannot be ruled out for an optimal concept that is not an either-or decision but instead, would be a combination of money supply orientation and inflation targeting," he said in a speech in Munich during May.

Like many other European bankers, Duisenberg points out that adopting a German-style approach to price stability would enhance the credibility of the ECB because the Bundesbank was so successful at curbing inflation.
In his speech last April, he made another important point.
"The ECB will probably not pursue an exchange rate objective...within the framework of keeping inflation in check, it would be useless to peg the euro to the dollar or the yen."
He said this was because monetary union would span a large and relatively closed area where the level of inflation would be determined by internal rather than external developments.
European bankers said there was one notable way in which the ECB would differ from the Bundesbank -- its members, drawn from EMU participants, would communicate with each other in English.
